title: Shadows and Shadow Culling Don't Render Properly on Asymmetrical Cameras
body:
### Tested versions

Reproducible in: 
- v4.8.dev.custom_build
- v4.7.2.stable.official
- v4.7.1.stable.official
- v4.6.3.stable.official
- v4.5.2.stable.official
- v4.4.1.stable.official
- Probably older versions too, but I did not check anything older than v4.4.1

### System information

Godot v4.7.2.stable - Windows 11 (build 26200) - Multi-window, 3 monitors - Direct3D 12 (Forward+) - dedicated NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (NVIDIA; 32.0.16.1656) - AMD Ryzen 9 7950X 16-Core Processor (32 threads) - 63.11 GiB memory - WASAPI (48000 Hz, Stereo/mono)

### Issue description

When using Projection Mode Frustum, a small size, and a small frustum offset, shadows and shadow culling do not work as expected. Attached you will see a simple scene setup with a large cube that casts shadows and then what that scene looks like through an asymmetrical camera. 

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/51a65004-445d-481f-b1ce-41a31a82dea8



### Steps to reproduce

- Create an empty scene.
- Add Node
- Add DirectionalLight3D
- Set rotation to (-33, 0, 0)
- Turn Shadows On
- Add WorldEnvironment
- Create new Environment for WorldEnvironment
- Add Camera3D
- Set Projection Mode to Frustum
- Set Size to 0.032
- Set Frustum Offset.x to -0.058
- Set position to (0, 2, 0)
- Add MeshInstance3D
- Set Mesh to Plane
- Set Plane size to x=100 y=100
- Add MeshInstance3D
- Set Mesh to Box
- Set Box size to x=50, y=50
- Set Box position to (-30, 0, 46)

Add the following scrip to Camera3D:
```
extends Camera3D

@export var mouse_sensitivity := 0.002

var yaw := 0.0
var pitch := 0.0

func _ready() -> void:
	Input.mouse_mode = Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED

func _input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event is InputEventMouseMotion:
		yaw -= event.relative.x * mouse_sensitivity
		pitch -= event.relative.y * mouse_sensitivity
		pitch = clamp(pitch, -PI / 2.0, PI / 2.0)

		rotation = Vector3(pitch, yaw, 0.0)
```

(Really you just need a way to rotate the camera around)

Play scene. You should see shadows messed up.

Ultimately, you just need a directional light that casts shadows, objects in a scene that have shadows/receive shadows, and a camera set to Frustum with a size/offset ratio of roughly 0.5. I have personally found that the size/offset I list here is just one of the easier ones to spot the problem with as if things get too stretched it can be hard to tell what's accurate and what's not. I haven't tested much beyond the ratio of 0.5 between size and offset. It seems to be the sweet spot (or bad spot I suppose), but can't confirm.
